title: "Influence"

Leverage measures unusual predictor position. [**Influence**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85) asks how much the fitted result changes when an observation, or a scientifically meaningful group of observations, is removed.

One Provo row is an [aggregated, fixation-contingent word position](regression-models.qmd#provo-word-position-data), and its predictor is modeled cloze surprisal, the negative base-two logarithm of a fitted cloze probability. Row influence therefore concerns a position rather than a reader. Passage deletion keeps together the positions that share one passage context.

The [residual](residuals.qmd) supplies observed-minus-fitted response information, while response [variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) sets its scale. In the Bayesian calculation, a [posterior distribution](../statistical-inference/posterior-distributions.qmd) is the parameter distribution after conditioning on the observed responses; deletion changes that conditioning set.

Cook's distance combines predictor position with residual size for one row. Because the Provo positions remain grouped within passages, a whole-passage deletion asks a second and scientifically better aligned sensitivity question.

## Cook's distance and grouped deletion

For a Gaussian linear model with $p$ coefficients and residual variance estimate $s^2$, Cook's distance for position $i$ is

$$
D_i
=
\frac{e_i^2}{ps^2}
\frac{h_{ii}}{(1-h_{ii})^2}.
$$

Cook's distance can also be read as the scaled change in the fitted vector:

$$
D_i
=
\frac{
\sum_j(\widehat y_j-\widehat y_{j(i)})^2
}{ps^2},
$$

where $\widehat y_{j(i)}$ is the fitted value after deleting row $i$. The closed form above avoids $n$ separate refits by combining the row's residual with its leverage. The [leverage page](leverage-and-influence.qmd) supplies the design component; the residual supplies disagreement with the fitted mean.

Large residuals and high leverage can jointly produce a large $D_i$. But the Provo regression retains passages as a grouping unit, so deleting one position is not the only relevant perturbation. We also refit after deleting each whole passage.

```{r}
#| label: compute-provo-influence
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv(
  "data/provo/content-word-positions.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
provo$cloze_surprisal_bits <- -log2(provo$OrthoMatchModel)
provo$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  provo$cloze_surprisal_bits - mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits)
fit <- lm(mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_c, data = provo)
provo$cooks_distance <- cooks.distance(fit)

full_slope <- coef(fit)[["cloze_surprisal_c"]]
passage_deletion <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  sort(unique(provo$Text_ID)),
  function(current_passage) {
    reduced_fit <- lm(
      mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_c,
      data = subset(provo, Text_ID != current_passage)
    )
    reduced_slope <- coef(reduced_fit)[["cloze_surprisal_c"]]
    data.frame(
      deleted_passage = current_passage,
      deleted_positions = sum(provo$Text_ID == current_passage),
      slope_without_passage = reduced_slope,
      slope_change = reduced_slope - full_slope
    )
  }
))
passage_deletion$absolute_change <- abs(passage_deletion$slope_change)
most_influential_passage <- passage_deletion$deleted_passage[
  which.max(passage_deletion$absolute_change)
]
fit_without_passage <- lm(
  mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_c,
  data = subset(provo, Text_ID != most_influential_passage)
)

stopifnot(nrow(passage_deletion) == length(unique(provo$Text_ID)))

passage_deletion[order(-passage_deletion$absolute_change), ][1:6, ]
```

The most influential individual position and its retained measurement fields are:

```{r}
#| label: inspect-most-influential-provo-position
provo[which.max(provo$cooks_distance), c(
  "position_id", "Text_ID", "Word_Number", "Word_POS", "Word_Length",
  "mean_log_ffd", "cloze_surprisal_bits", "cooks_distance"
)]
```

The largest whole-passage deletion changes the slope by `r sprintf("%.6f", passage_deletion$slope_change[which.max(passage_deletion$absolute_change)])` log milliseconds per bit. This change is computed by removing passage `r most_influential_passage`, not by inventing a perturbation.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-influence
#| fig-cap: "Observed Provo positions with the full fit in blue and the fit after deleting the most slope-influential passage in black."
grid <- data.frame(
  cloze_surprisal_bits = seq(
    min(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    max(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    length.out = 160L
  )
)
grid$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  grid$cloze_surprisal_bits - mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits)
grid$full_fit <- predict(fit, newdata = grid)
grid$deleted_fit <- predict(fit_without_passage, newdata = grid)

point_opacity <- 0.18
ggplot(provo, aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, mean_log_ffd)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey70", alpha = point_opacity, size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(y = full_fit), color = "#2C6E9B", linewidth = 0.85) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(y = deleted_fit), color = "black", linetype = 2) +
  labs(
    x = "Modeled cloze surprisal (bits)",
    y = "Mean log first-fixation duration"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The two lines remain close. That stability is specific to the fitted Provo regression slope under these passage deletions. It does not show that the missing reader-level grouping is unimportant.

Deleting the most influential passage is a sensitivity analysis: it asks whether one grouped source carries the slope. It is not a data-cleaning instruction. A deletion would require separate evidence that the measurement or inclusion rule was wrong. The relevant generalization target is new passages, so whole-passage perturbations complement the row-level Cook calculation.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Why does Cook's distance combine residual size and leverage?
2. Which deletion unit matches the remaining Provo regression grouping structure?
3. What would a large passage-level slope change imply?
4. Why is influence a diagnostic rather than a deletion command?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Residual size measures disagreement with the fitted line, while leverage measures capacity to move it; Cook's distance is large when those features act together. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Deleting a whole passage matches the remaining grouping structure marked by `Text_ID`. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. A large passage-level slope change would show that the fitted surprisal slope is sensitive to evidence concentrated in that passage. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Influence identifies consequential observations or groups for investigation; deletion requires a separate measurement or design justification. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

The [next page](bayesian-linear-regression.qmd) places a posterior distribution over the same line.
